71.title: The brothers come for bread (Genesis 42)
71.hook: they bow to a man they don't recognize
71.carry: you don't see who it is
71.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads this chapter as the beginning of the brothers' repair: the first time they admit aloud what they did to Joseph.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner put in charge of Egypt's grain. Your line was store in the good years. Now the lean years arrive. Day seventy-one.

The famine spreads past Egypt, all the way to Canaan, to Jacob's tents. And Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt. He says to his sons, why are you staring at each other? Go down and buy us food, so we can live. Ten brothers go. Not Benjamin. Jacob won't let Rachel's last son out of his sight. So ten men walk into Egypt with money in their bags, and stand in line in front of the governor who sells the grain to everyone. And they bow down to him, faces to the ground. Just like the sheaves in a dream they once laughed at. Today: the man they don't recognize.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS, NOT BENJAMIN.` → `FACES TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The Torah puts the whole scene in one line: "And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew him not." How could they not know him? He was seventeen when they sold him, and now he's nearly forty. He's shaved like an Egyptian, dressed like one, speaks through an interpreter. An old explanation, passed on by Rashi, says it simply: when they sold him he had no beard, and now he had one. But there's a deeper reason. They weren't looking for him. You don't see who it is when you've decided who it can't be. And Joseph? He remembers the dreams. He speaks to them harshly. The Hebrew here is clever: he recognized them, and made himself a stranger to them, and those two verbs come from the same root. He calls them spies. They protest: we are twelve brothers, sons of one man; the youngest is with our father, and one is no more. One is no more. They're talking about him, to his face. Joseph keeps one brother, Simeon, as a hostage, and says: bring me your youngest brother. And then, thinking the governor can't understand Hebrew, the brothers say to each other: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother," we saw his distress when he pleaded with us, and we wouldn't listen. Reuben says, didn't I tell you? And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away from them and weeps. Twenty years later, the brothers are finally talking about what they did. And the man they did it to is standing right there, listening.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice someone you may have misjudged. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've filed away. The difficult coworker. The relative you've written off. The stranger you decided about in one glance. Ask yourself what you might not be seeing. What they might be carrying, or who they might have become since. You don't have to change your mind. Just leave the door open a crack. The bell holds the time.
The brothers come for bread. Ten brothers bow to the governor of Egypt, and never see that he's the brother they sold.
screen: `THE BROTHERS COME FOR BREAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you don't see who it is. Today, look again at one person you think you already know. Day seventy-one.

72.title: The silver cup (Genesis 44:1–17)
72.hook: the test: will the brothers abandon another favorite son?
72.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls turning around teshuvah, and Maimonides' test for it, facing the same situation and choosing differently, is often taught through this story, especially in the season before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers come for bread, and bow to a man they don't recognize. Your line was you don't see who it is. Did you look again at someone? Day seventy-two.

The grain runs out, and the brothers have to go back to Egypt. This time they bring Benjamin, because the governor demanded it. Jacob lets him go only after Judah promises: I'll be responsible for him. If I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. In Egypt, the governor invites them to a feast. Simeon is released. Benjamin gets five times as much food as anyone else. The favorite son, again, getting more, right in front of the others. And the brothers seem fine with it. They eat and drink and relax. The next morning they head for home, sacks full. Today: what's hidden in Benjamin's sack.
screen: `THEY BRING BENJAMIN.` → `FIVE TIMES AS MUCH FOR HIM.` → `SACKS FULL, HEADING HOME.`

segments.voice: Before they leave, Joseph gives his steward an order: put my silver cup in the youngest one's sack. They're barely out of the city when the steward catches up. Why have you repaid good with evil? You stole my master's cup! The brothers are so sure of themselves they make a reckless offer: whoever has it, let him die, and the rest of us will be slaves. The steward searches, oldest to youngest. Sack after sack. And it's in Benjamin's. The brothers tear their clothes, the same thing Jacob did over Joseph's coat, and every one of them turns around and goes back to the city. That's the moment. Nobody has to go back. The governor then makes them the easiest offer in the world: only the one who had the cup will be my slave. The rest of you, go home in peace. It's the pit all over again. A favored son of Rachel. A chance to be rid of him, and to tell their father something sad but blameless. And Judah speaks for all of them: "God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants." He doesn't argue about the cup. He's thinking of an older guilt. And they refuse to leave Benjamin. Maimonides, the great medieval teacher, describes complete repentance, teshuvah, this way. It's when you find yourself in the same situation, with the same pull, the same chance, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't, but because you've changed. The silver cup is that test. Twenty-two years ago these brothers sold a favorite son. Today they won't.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by someone when it costs you. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who might need you on their side right now. A friend people are talking about. A coworker taking the blame. A family member who's the odd one out. Picture yourself standing next to them. What would it cost you? A little comfort, some awkwardness, a bit of your reputation? Hold that cost honestly. Then decide if you'll pay it. The bell holds the time.
The silver cup. Hidden in Benjamin's sack as a test, to see whether the brothers would abandon another favorite son. They wouldn't.
Your line: not this time. Today, when an old habit shows up, the one you've been trying to leave behind, say those words, and choose differently. Day seventy-two.

73.title: Judah's plea (Genesis 44:18–34)
73.hook: Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place
73.howItsDone: Judah's plea opens the weekly Torah portion Vayigash, read in synagogue each winter, and Jewish teaching holds him up as the model of someone who truly changed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silver cup: the same chance to abandon a favorite son, and the brothers refused. Your line was not this time. Today, the brother who once said sell him steps forward. Day seventy-three.

Picture the room. The governor of Egypt, the most powerful man any of them has ever met, has just said: the one with the cup stays as my slave, the rest of you go. The brothers are on the floor. Benjamin is standing there, the cup found in his bag, his whole life about to be taken away. And the Torah says: "Then Judah came near unto him." In Hebrew, one word, vayigash, and he drew near. Nobody tells him to. Nobody expects him to. Judah, who years ago looked at another brother in a pit and said, let's sell him, walks up to the most dangerous man in the room. Today: what he says.
screen: `THE ONE WITH THE CUP STAYS.` → `THEN JUDAH CAME NEAR.` → `THE BROTHER WHO SAID SELL HIM.`

segments.voice: Judah's speech is one of the longest in the book of Genesis, and it isn't clever. It's a story. He tells the governor about their old father. About the son of his old age, whose brother is dead, the only one left from his mother, and whom his father loves. He quotes his father's own words: you know my wife bore me two sons; one went out from me, and I said, surely he is torn in pieces, and I haven't seen him since. If you take this one too, and harm comes to him, you'll bring my gray hairs down with sorrow to the grave. Listen to what Judah is doing. He's saying out loud that his father loves Benjamin more. He's accepting it. The jealousy that sold Joseph is gone. And then the offer: "let thy servant, I pray thee, abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren." Take me instead. I'll be your slave for the rest of my life. And the last line: "For how shall I go up to my father, if the lad be not with me?" Think about who's hearing this. Joseph. The brother who was sold into slavery is now listening to the man who sold him offer to become a slave, so that a brother, and a father, won't suffer what Joseph and Jacob suffered. The rabbis honor Judah as the model of turning around, teshuvah. And the Jewish people came to be named after him: Judah, Yehudah, gave us the word Jew.
screen: `VAYIGASH: AND HE DREW NEAR.` · `OUR FATHER LOVES HIM.` · `LET ME STAY INSTEAD OF THE LAD.` · `JUDAH, YEHUDAH, JEW.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL I GO UP TO MY FATHER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer to carry someone's load. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone near you who's carrying too much right now. A parent with a sick kid. A friend in a hard month. A coworker buried in work. Think of one concrete thing you could take off their hands. A meal, a ride, a shift, an afternoon of childcare. Not a vague let me know. A real offer. Decide who and what. The bell holds the time.
Judah's plea. The brother who once said sell him draws near and offers himself as a slave, so that Benjamin can go home.
Your line: take me instead. Today, make one real offer to carry something for someone, and mean it. Day seventy-three.

74.title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45:1–15)
74.hook: he weeps so loudly Egypt hears; "it was not you that sent me hither, but God"
74.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads Joseph's words as a model of forgiveness that names the wrong honestly, and Jewish teachers also stress that forgiving does not require pretending a harm was good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah's plea: the brother who said sell him offered to be a slave so Benjamin could go home. Your line was take me instead. Did you make an offer? Day seventy-four.

Judah finishes speaking, and the room goes quiet. The governor can't hold it anymore. He shouts at his servants: everyone out! Clear the room! The Egyptian guards and attendants file out, and the door closes on eleven frightened Hebrew shepherds and one Egyptian lord. Then he starts crying. Not quietly. The text says he wept so loudly that the Egyptians outside heard it, and word reached Pharaoh's house. The brothers have no idea what's happening. They think they're about to be enslaved. Today: two words that change everything.
screen: `EVERYONE OUT!` → `HE WEEPS SO LOUD EGYPT HEARS.` → `THE BROTHERS DON'T UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: Then, in Hebrew, with no interpreter now: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" Ani Yosef. And the brothers can't answer. The text says they were terrified at his presence. The rabbis noticed that silence. One old teacher said: if the brothers couldn't answer Joseph when he spoke one sentence, how will any of us answer on the day we're shown our whole lives? Joseph sees their fear, and says: come near to me, please. And they come near. I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. He says it. He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. And then: don't be grieved, and don't be angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to preserve life. Two years of famine, five more to come, and I'm here to keep you alive. And the line the whole story has been building to: "So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God." What is Joseph doing? Readers disagree, honestly. Some hear real forgiveness: he's found a meaning in his suffering, and he frees his brothers from the weight of it. Others notice that he's reframing it for himself, that he needed this story to survive. And the Torah doesn't say the brothers were off the hook; years later, they're still afraid of him. What the text does show is a man looking back over the pit, the slavery, the prison, and seeing a path. Not a good thing. A road that led somewhere. Then he kisses all his brothers, and weeps on them. "And after that his brethren talked with him." For the first time since the coat.
screen: `I AM JOSEPH.` · `THE BROTHERS CAN'T ANSWER.` · `COME NEAR TO ME.` · `NOT YOU THAT SENT ME, BUT GOD.` · then, large: `AND AFTER THAT HIS BRETHREN TALKED WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reframe one old hurt, gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard that happened to you a while ago. Not your deepest wound; something you've had time with. Ask one question: did it lead anywhere? A strength, a friend, a path you wouldn't have found. You don't have to say it was good, or that anyone was right to do it. Some hurts don't reframe, and that's allowed. Just look for the road. The bell holds the time.
I am Joseph. Ani Yosef. Two words, after twenty-two years, and the brothers finally see who has been standing in front of them.
Your line: it led somewhere. Today, when you remember a hard chapter, look for one thing it taught you or led you to. Day seventy-four.

75.title: Blessing the grandsons (Genesis 48)
75.hook: Jacob blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, whose names parents still use to bless children on Friday night
75.howItsDone: On Friday night many Jewish parents place their hands on their children's heads and bless them, sons with the names of Ephraim and Manasseh and daughters with Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah, followed by the priestly blessing from Numbers 6.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I am Joseph: two words, a flood of tears, and a hard road seen as a path. Your line was it led somewhere. Since then, Jacob has come down to Egypt and held his lost son again. Now he's old. Day seventy-five.

On Friday night, in Jewish homes all over the world, something happens right before dinner. The candles are lit. The table's set. And a parent puts their hands on a child's head, sometimes a toddler squirming, sometimes a teenager rolling their eyes, sometimes a grown child home for the weekend. And they say a blessing. For a son, it starts with two names that most people outside the tradition have never heard. Not Abraham. Not Moses. Two boys born in Egypt. Today: where that blessing comes from.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT, BEFORE DINNER.` → `HANDS ON A CHILD'S HEAD.` → `TWO NAMES FROM EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Jacob is sick, near the end, his eyes dim. Joseph brings his two sons to him, Manasseh the older and Ephraim the younger. And the old man says something that sums up his whole life: "I had not thought to see thy face; and, lo, God hath let me see thy seed also." He thought Joseph was dead, torn by a wild animal. Now he's holding his grandchildren. Joseph places them carefully: the older at Jacob's right hand, the younger at his left. And Jacob crosses his arms. Right hand on the younger, Ephraim. Left on the older. Joseph tries to fix it. Jacob refuses: I know, my son, I know. The younger will be greater. It's the old pattern of Genesis, younger before older, Jacob before Esau. But this time, notice: no stolen blessing, no fight. Manasseh doesn't storm off. Then Jacob says: "By thee shall Israel bless, saying: God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." And that's exactly what Jewish parents do, thousands of years later. Why these two? Commentators give different answers. Some say they're the first brothers in Genesis who didn't fight each other. Others say they were born and raised in Egypt, far from home, and still stayed who they were. For daughters, parents name the four mothers: Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. And then, for all of them, the old priestly blessing: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."
screen: `I HAD NOT THOUGHT TO SEE THY FACE.` · `JACOB CROSSES HIS HANDS.` · `GOD MAKE THEE AS EPHRAIM AND MANASSEH.` · `BROTHERS WHO DIDN'T FIGHT.` · then, large: `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a child or a younger person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone younger in your life. Your own kid, a niece, a student, a new coworker. Picture them clearly. If you pray, you can hold them in the old words: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee. If not, think of one good thing you see in them, something true, and imagine saying it to them. Later today, you might. The bell holds the time.
Blessing the grandsons. Jacob crosses his hands over Ephraim and Manasseh, and their names become the blessing Jewish parents still give.
Your line: may you be like them. Today, tell one younger person a good thing you see in them. Say it plainly. Day seventy-five.

76.title: Genesis ends (Genesis 49–50)
76.hook: Jacob's blessings, Joseph's forgiveness, and a coffin waiting to go home; finishing a book, the synagogue says "be strong"
76.tomorrow: a king who knew not Joseph
76.howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation stands and calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek, and the reader repeats it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing the grandsons: Jacob's crossed hands, and a blessing parents still say on Friday night. Your line was may you be like them. Today, the last page of the first book. Day seventy-six.

Picture a synagogue on a Saturday morning in winter. The Torah scroll is open on the table, and the reader is chanting the very last verse of Genesis. The whole book, from let there be light to here, is about to be finished. And the moment the last word is sung, the whole room stands up and calls out together, three words, loud: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another. It's a little like the cheer at the end of a long race. Today: how the book ends, and why people shout.
screen: `THE LAST VERSE OF GENESIS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.`

segments.voice: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and blesses them one by one. The blessings are honest; some are praise, some are hard words about old wrongs. Then he asks to be buried with his fathers in the cave at Hebron, and he dies. Joseph and his brothers carry him home, with a great Egyptian procession, and bury him. And then, walking back to Egypt, the brothers get scared. Maybe now that Father is gone, Joseph will pay us back. They send him a message, and they fall down before him. And Joseph weeps, and says: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God? And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." He'll take care of them, and their little ones. Seventeen years of peace after the reunion, and they still needed to hear it again. Sometimes forgiveness has to be said twice. Then Joseph grows old, and he asks one thing: when God brings you out of here, carry my bones with you. And Genesis ends with this line: "and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." The book that began with a garden ends with a coffin in a foreign land, waiting to go home. That's where the chazak comes in. Chazak means be strong. The tradition says it at the end of every one of the five books of the Torah, and it makes sense here most of all. We've finished something long. The ending isn't tidy. And the next book begins in slavery. So before you turn the page: be strong, be strong, and strengthen each other.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one small thing, and say chazak. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small you've left undone. A drawer, an email, a chapter of a book, a thank-you note, a dish in the sink. Choose it. When the bell ends, go and finish it. And when it's done, say the word, even quietly: chazak. Be strong. Look back, too, at this part of the path: Rachel's grave, the coat, the pit, Tamar, the prison, the dreams, the cup, Judah, I am Joseph, the grandsons. You finished it. The bell holds the time.
Chazak. Be strong. Called out in synagogue when a book of the Torah is finished: chazak, chazak, venitchazek.
Your line: be strong, be strong. Today, when you finish anything, even something small, say chazak, and tell someone else the same. Day seventy-six.

77.title: A king who knew not Joseph (Exodus 1:8–14)
77.word: A king who knew not Joseph
77.hook: a new Pharaoh, fear of a growing people, and slavery
77.howItsDone: The book of Exodus, Shemot in Hebrew, begins its synagogue reading each winter, and its story of slavery and freedom is retold at the Passover seder every spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chazak: Genesis ended with a coffin in Egypt, and the whole room saying be strong. Your line was be strong, be strong. This week took us from brothers bowing for bread, through the cup, Judah's plea and I am Joseph, to the end of a book. Today, a new one opens. Day seventy-seven.

The second book of the Torah is called Shemot, Names, because it opens by listing the names of Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt. Seventy people. Then Joseph dies, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. And their children have children, and the text piles up the words: they were fruitful, they swarmed, they multiplied, they grew very strong, and the land was filled with them. A family has become a people. Then one short verse turns everything: "Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph." Today: what a man who forgets can do.
screen: `SHEMOT: NAMES.` → `SEVENTY BECOME A PEOPLE.` → `A NEW KING OVER EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Who knew not Joseph. How could a Pharaoh not know the man who saved Egypt from famine? The Talmud records two answers. One rabbi says: it really was a new king. The other says: it was the same king, who made new decrees, and acted as if he'd never known Joseph. Forgetting on purpose. Then listen to his speech to his people. The children of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. "Come, let us deal wisely with them," in case there's a war, and they join our enemies. Notice what's happened. Nobody has done anything. There's no crime, no rebellion. There's only a number, and a fear of what that number might do someday. And from fear comes a plan. First, taskmasters and forced labor: they build the store cities of Pithom and Raamses. Then the Torah says something almost defiant: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied." And the Egyptians, the text says, came to dread them. So the labor gets harder. Mortar, brick, work in the fields, all of it made bitter. This is how the whole story of the Exodus begins. Not with a monster. With a man who forgot what someone had done for his country, looked at a group of neighbors, and saw a threat. Jews tell this story every year at the Passover seder, and teachers have long noticed how ordinary its first step is. Forgetting. Then fear. Then cruelty that feels, to the people doing it, like being wise.
screen: `A NEW KING, OR ONE WHO CHOSE TO FORGET?` · `TOO MANY AND TOO MIGHTY FOR US.` · `LET US DEAL WISELY WITH THEM.` · `THE MORE THEY AFFLICTED, THE MORE THEY GREW.` · then, large: `FEAR FORGETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where fear turns into cruelty. Settle, and breathe. Think about the last time you heard someone talk about a group of people as a threat. Too many of them. They'll take over. Maybe you heard it on the news. Maybe you've thought it. Notice what the fear was based on. Something they did, or something someone imagined they might do? You don't have to settle anything. Just see the first step. The bell holds the time.
A king who knew not Joseph. A new Pharaoh forgets what Joseph did for Egypt, fears a growing people, and makes them slaves.
screen: `A KING WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: fear forgets. Today, when you feel afraid of a group of people, stop and remember one good thing someone from that group has done. Day seventy-seven.

fork.setup: you're Pharaoh's advisor. a foreign people in your land is growing fast. they've done nothing wrong. Pharaoh asks what to do.
options: welcome them; their ancestor saved Egypt.
deal wisely with them before they grow stronger.
send them home to Canaan.
fork.reveal: Pharaoh chooses "come, let us deal wisely with them": taskmasters, forced labor, and slavery. fear, dressed up as wisdom.

original.note: Hebrew: names. the Hebrew title of the book of Exodus, from its opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a new king who never heard of Joseph.
what it means: a king who forgot, or chose to forget, and turned fear of neighbors into slavery.
what a scholar hears: Sotah 11a: Rav and Shmuel disagree: a truly new king, or the same king with new decrees. Rashi on 1:8 cites both.
